query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new combined atomistic simulation and Boltzmann transport approach that explicitly decouples the lattice and electronic thermal conduction in HfNbTaTiZr can predict each contribution separately with significantly lower error than earlier conflated analytical estimates.
generation.material_initial_state: Defect‐free, near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy in bulk form.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply an approach that uses DFT-derived elastic and vibrational properties to compute lattice thermal conductivity (including an explicit, temperature‐dependent Debye temperature treatment) and separately employs electronic structure calculations to model the electronic contribution via Boltzmann transport theory.
generation.conditions: Predictions are to be compared against experiments on pure (oxygen‐free) specimens from ~300 K up to 1200 K for the lattice component and against low temperature (<200 K) measurements where the electronic part becomes comparable to lattice conduction.
generation.structural_mediator: The high configurational disorder and resulting phonon scattering in the high-entropy alloy are captured in the modified vibrational density of states and elastic tensors derived from DFT, acting as mediators between the alloy’s atomic structure and its heat transport mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: By decoupling the contributions, the method avoids the error introduced by applying a single Debye temperature to a composite conduction model. The detailed atomic-scale modeling yields improved estimates of thermal transport: the lattice part is computed by advanced vibrational property modeling while the electronic part is evaluated independently using calculated scattering rates and transport coefficients.
generation.predicted_outcome: The approach will yield lattice thermal conductivity values that agree with experiments within ±10% across 300–1200 K, and will separately predict an electronic contribution consistent with low temperature (<200 K) conduction measurements. Overall, the decoupled predictions will reduce the combined error by roughly 15–20% relative to earlier conflated analytical methods.
generation.baseline: Earlier models treated the alloy as a perfect, defect-free bulk crystal and used a single Debye parameter or simplified estimates that conflated lattice and electronic contributions, leading to uncertainties and inaccuracies.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to hold in high-purity, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr samples in the temperature range 100–1200 K; its accuracy might diminish in specimens with significant oxygen contamination or other defects, and at temperatures well outside this range.
generation.uncertainty: The exact improvement margin (estimated at 15–20% reduction in error) and the precise decoupling efficacy at the boundary temperatures retain an uncertainty of about ±5% due to possible variations in sample quality and measurement challenges.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare high-purity, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr samples; perform temperature-dependent thermal conductivity measurements from ~100 K to 1200 K. Separate the total conductivity into lattice and electronic components using standard techniques (e.g., applying the Wiedemann-Franz law at low temperatures to extract the electronic contribution). Independently run the new simulation approach to predict the lattice and electronic components.
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity across the 300–1200 K range
Total thermal conductivity below 200 K with separation into electronic and lattice parts
Comparison of predicted and measured values for both components
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted lattice and electronic thermal conductivities differ from the corresponding experimental measurements by more than ±10% across the specified temperature ranges, or if the overall error reduction relative to previous estimates is less than approximately 15%, then the hypothesis is falsified.
